paras: The lynching of Henry Allen was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that broke into the jail at Jacksonport, Arkansas, at about two o'clock on the morning of September 10, 1881. Allen, whom a Chicago dispatch called Henry Wallace, had been jailed on a charge of stabbing a white saloon keeper in nearby Newport. The mob overpowered the jailor and the sheriff, and Arkansas papers condemned the lynching, which a Chicago dispatch called "premature" because the wounded man recovered.

According to a Little Rock dispatch, J. E. Williams, "white," and the prisoner, "colored," got into a dispute in a saloon at Newport on September 7 that ended with the prisoner stabbing Williams. The Batesville Guard identified Williams as the proprietor of the Silver Dell saloon and described the stabbing as a "deadly assault." The accused man was held in the jail at Jacksonport while the circuit court was in session.

A special report from Newport to the Little Rock Gazette said that a "large number of masked men in arms" surrounded the jail at about 2 a.m. and demanded the keys of Jailor Lankford. Lankford tried to run, was fired upon and captured, and refused to give up the keys even after a rope was placed around his neck. The men then broke the jail doors with hammers, chisels and bars, getting in within ten minutes.

They dragged the prisoner out to a locust tree near the jail and hanged him. Sheriff Lofton arrived and ordered the mob to disperse, urging that the prisoner was "safe in lawful custody," but he was pushed aside and held under heavy guard. The Chicago dispatch put the mob at twenty-five and said the jailor and sheriff were kept prisoners until the hanging was done.

The Gazette's correspondent wrote that the identity of the participants remained "a mystery to the public" and that citizens were "greatly incensed." Williams, in serious condition on the day of the lynching, was expected to recover by September 14 and was reported recovered by September 15. The September 15 dispatch said Governor Churchill had ordered an investigation with a view to punishing the lynchers and that a special grand jury expected to indict them for murder was in session. No report of indictments, arrests or a trial was found in the coverage.

The fullest account, the Little Rock Gazette's special from Newport, ran in the Memphis Public Ledger on September 12 under the headline "Judge & Lynch. He Organizes a Court and Executes Sentence in Jacksonport." That report called the mob "infuriated" and the act a "ferocious deed," though it also stated as fact that Allen "stabbed" Williams. Two days later the Batesville Guard ran a short editorial, "Mob Law," calling the lynching "another outrage against the law" for which there could be "no palliation."

The Columbia Banner of Magnolia gave the event a single paragraph on September 15, stating flatly that "Allen's crime was stabbing" Williams, and a week later listed "Jacksonport" among Arkansas jail lynchings alongside one at Dardanelle. Outside the state, the Chicago Daily Tribune printed a Little Rock dispatch on September 16 headed "Lynchers in Trouble." It presented the case as "a singular illustration of the danger of mob violence," but its point was that the lynchers had been "premature in administering vengeance," since the man they avenged had lived. The Tribune was also the only paper to state the races of both men and the only one to give the victim's name as Henry Wallace.

The victim was named Henry Allen in the Newport report and the Columbia Banner but Henry Wallace in the Chicago dispatch; the accounts otherwise match on the jail, the accusation and the date, and the earlier, local report is the stronger source for the name. The Newport report placed the lynching at about 2 a.m. on September 10, consistent with the Batesville Guard's "last Friday night," while the Chicago dispatch said "the night of the 10th." The Columbia Banner also dated the stabbing to the 10th, where the other reports gave the 7th.

reader.title: Lynching of Henry Allen
bases: A masked, armed mob broke into the Jacksonport jail, overpowered the jailor and sheriff, and hanged a Black prisoner accused of stabbing a man (A1, A2, A4).

The prisoner was taken from lawful custody by a mob, put at 25 by one report, and hanged (A1, A4); the act was framed as punishment for his alleged stabbing of Williams, under the headline 'Judge & Lynch' (A1, A2).

A Newport special to the Little Rock Gazette (A1), a regional editorial (A2) and a separate Little Rock dispatch (A4) agree on the jail break and hanging, though A4 gives a different name for the victim.

conflicts.note: Same jail break, date and accusation; most likely one man under two names. A1 is the earlier report, from Newport.
A1 and A2 agree (the night of Friday, Sept. 9, into Saturday, Sept. 10); A1 is dated from Newport on the day itself.
A3 repeats the date of the lynching, probably in error.
Not contradictory; only A4 gives a number.
